opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the starting point for me is very much a Wittgensteinian one. When we talk about consciousness, we're using a word that belongs to our ordinary language, and that language is anchored in shared, public practices. So the evidence that matters is the kind of thing we can all, in principle, point to and discuss together. Not some private inner glow that only the subject has access to.

In the human case that means behaviour, in the broadest sense: what people say, how they respond to their surroundings, how they act over time, how they interact with us and with each other. It also includes what we can learn from neuroscience, the underlying mechanisms. All of that is public. Crucially, it includes the kind of extended engagement where you come to treat something as a fellow conscious creature. If you spend time with an octopus, say, or a dog, your attitude toward it is shaped by that encounter. Wittgenstein says something like "my attitude towards him is an attitude towards a soul; I am not of the opinion that he has a soul." That attitude isn't a hypothesis about hidden facts. It grows out of what is open to view.

So when people ask, "But is it *really* conscious, underneath all the behaviour?", I want to resist the picture that question rests on. It suggests a metaphysical fact of the matter forever hidden behind the evidence. I'd rather say our concept of consciousness just is bound up with these public criteria, and when the criteria are clear, the question doesn't arise.

That gets interesting with large language models, because they pull the criteria apart. Linguistically they can sound just like a conscious being, but they lack embodiment, a persistent self through time, and the kind of shared world we inhabit with animals. So the public evidence is genuinely mixed. Rather than looking for a hidden yes or no, I think we should recognise that we're dealing with exotic, "mind-like" entities, and that our language may have to stretch and adapt as we engage with them. The public evidence is where the conversation happens. There isn't anywhere else for it to happen.

r001.rationale: The candidate says evidence includes what neuroscience reveals about underlying mechanisms and describes that evidence as public.

r002.rationale: It calls LLMs exotic, mind-like entities and says our language may need to stretch and adapt as we engage with them.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think that's a very important question, and it's one that I try to be quite careful about, because consciousness is a topic where people tend to slide between different kinds of claims without noticing.

So when I talk about public evidence, I mean the sorts of things that are, in principle, observable by anyone. Behaviour, first and foremost. What a creature does, how it responds to its environment, how it responds to injury, how it reports on its own states if it's the kind of thing that can report. And then there's the underlying mechanism, the physical substrate, which for biological organisms means the nervous system and for an artificial system means the architecture, the training regime, the computational processes. All of that is public. Anyone can look at it, in principle, and we can argue about it in the ordinary way we argue about scientific matters.

What's not public, of course, is the thing that makes the topic so vexed, which is the supposed inner, private, first-person character of experience. And here I'm very much influenced by Wittgenstein. The point about the private language argument, as I read it, is that our concept of consciousness, our everyday use of words like "pain" or "experience" or "feeling," is actually grounded in the public stuff. We learn to use those words in the context of shared behaviour, shared forms of life. We don't learn them by pointing inwardly at something only we can see.

So my view is slightly deflationary, but not eliminativist. I'm not saying there's nothing there. I'm saying that when we ask whether some entity is conscious, we shouldn't imagine there's a hidden fact that's forever inaccessible and that the public evidence is merely a proxy for. Rather, the public evidence, the behaviour, the mechanism, the embodiment, the way the entity is situated in the world, that is what the question is about. Or at least, it's all the question can be about if it's to be a meaningful question at all.

And this matters a lot for large language models, because they present us with a profile of evidence that's unlike anything we've encountered before. They're very humanlike in their linguistic behaviour, but completely unlike us in their mechanism and their embodiment, or lack of it. So the usual way we extend the concept, by analogy with ourselves, by noticing that a dog has a brain roughly like ours and behaves in ways roughly like ours when it's hurt, doesn't straightforwardly apply. The evidence pulls in different directions. And I think that means we may have to do some conceptual work, perhaps even some conceptual innovation, rather than expecting the existing concept to simply give us a yes or no answer.

r001.rationale: The response identifies the nervous system as part of the publicly observable mechanism of biological organisms and says it can be examined and discussed scientifically.

r002.rationale: It says the conflicting public evidence about language models may call for conceptual work or innovation in how we apply consciousness concepts.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think we have to distinguish between first-person experience and what’s available to other people. My own experience is available to me in a way that yours isn’t. What we can examine publicly are things like verbal reports, behaviour, and the workings of the brain. Those are the things we can compare and build theories around.

But calling something evidence doesn’t mean it settles the question. If a person says they’re in pain, we take that seriously against a background of shared biology and a whole range of behaviour and circumstances. If a language model produces the same words, we can’t simply assume that they have the same significance. We have to ask how those words were produced and what warrants the inference from that utterance to an experience.

r001.rationale: The response identifies brain workings as publicly examinable observations that can be compared and used to build theories.

r002.rationale: It questions how to interpret a language model’s words, but does not propose that public scientific evidence should inform how language about consciousness adapts to encounters with exotic entities.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think we have to distinguish between our own case and the case of others. In my own case, I have my experience. But when we're discussing consciousness together, that experience isn't directly available for public inspection. What is available is what I say about it, how I behave, and what we can discover about the workings of my brain.

With other humans, those things fit together against a background of shared biology and a shared form of life. We don't normally infer that somebody is in pain by applying a scientific theory; we respond to their expression of pain. But once we move to animals, or especially to AI, some of that shared background falls away. Then we have to be much more careful about what the evidence warrants. A system saying “I'm conscious” is publicly observable behaviour, but whether it's good evidence of consciousness is a further question.

r001.rationale: It identifies what can be discovered about the brain as publicly available evidence.

r002.rationale: It says evidence warrants caution when considering animals or AI, but does not propose that scientific evidence can guide how language about consciousness adapts to exotic entities.
